paragraphs: Active learning tries to reduce labeling costs by choosing which examples would be most useful to label next. Evaluating these choices is difficult when a method's apparent advantage depends on the kind of data or on a few favorable experimental runs. CDALBench addresses both sources of uncertainty in how active learning methods are compared.

The benchmark includes computer vision, natural language processing, and tabular learning tasks. It also provides an efficient greedy oracle that makes evaluation with 50 runs per experiment feasible. This combines breadth across application domains with enough repetitions to investigate how stable the comparisons are.

The results show that the strongest methods change across domains. They also show that conclusions based on only three runs can depend heavily on the selected random seeds: an established method can appear significantly better or significantly worse than random selection on the same dataset. The benchmark therefore makes the reliability of reported improvements part of the evaluation itself.
neurips-2024-a-cross-domain-benchmark-fo.tldr: CDALBench shows that active learning comparisons need both varied data domains and many repeated runs to establish reliable improvements.

paragraphs: Point cloud registration aligns two collections of 3D points using proposed matches between them. Incorrect matches can distort the estimated alignment, so identifying the trustworthy matches is a central part of the problem. This paper reformulates alignment as an ℓ0-minimization problem, organizing the search around local groups of correspondences built from a compatibility graph.

The algorithm separates two intertwined tasks in stages. First, it divides alignment error into rotation and translation fitting errors. It then uses null-space matrices to separate identifying reliable matches from estimating those transformations. This makes it possible to apply Bayesian reasoning to solve for the fitting errors. Matches with the smallest errors produce a candidate transformation for each local group.

The method selects the best candidate to perform registration. Experiments report robustness to high proportions of incorrect matches and to noise. Results on KITTI, 3DMatch, and 3DLoMatch show state-of-the-art performance against traditional and learning-based methods across the tested indoor and outdoor scenes.
neurips-2024-a-robust-inlier-identificat.tldr: The method identifies reliable point matches by separating alignment errors and transformation estimation, improving registration in noisy, outlier-heavy experiments.

paragraphs: An honest language model should recognize when it lacks the knowledge needed to answer and proactively decline in those cases. It should also remain willing to answer questions it can handle. This paper treats that balance as an alignment objective alongside helpfulness and harmlessness, making the model's knowledge boundaries central to the problem.

The authors establish a precise problem definition and formulate honesty using an idea inspired by the Analects of Confucius. They build metrics around that definition to quantify how a model's honesty changes after alignment. This gives the training objective an explicit evaluation framework: improvement must be assessed against a stated meaning of honesty.

The paper then introduces a flexible training framework and implements several efficient fine-tuning techniques. The reported experiments show substantial improvements on the proposed honesty metrics while preserving performance on other tasks. These findings support training models to manage their knowledge boundaries more effectively, with the measured gains specifically grounded in the paper's definition and evaluation of honesty.
neurips-2024-alignment-for-honesty-45793.tldr: The paper defines, measures, and trains language-model honesty as knowing when to answer and when to decline.

paragraphs: B-cos networks build explanations into their architecture by encouraging stronger alignment between inputs and model weights. Their decision explanations are faithful by design, and earlier versions achieved competitive classification performance. The practical obstacle was that these networks had to be trained from scratch, making the approach increasingly expensive for large pretrained models.

B-cosification converts an existing pretrained network into a B-cos version. The authors exploit architectural similarities between conventional and B-cos networks, studying conversion choices for both convolutional networks and vision transformers. This makes existing training investment useful when constructing an interpretable model.

The converted models can match the interpretability of B-cos networks trained from scratch while often achieving better classification performance at a fraction of the training cost. The authors also convert a pretrained CLIP model using limited data and computation. Its explanations remain highly interpretable, and its zero-shot performance is competitive across several datasets. These results extend the practical reach of architectural interpretability to pretrained models.
neurips-2024-b-cosification-transforming.tldr: B-cosification converts pretrained vision models into inherently interpretable versions while retaining competitive performance and reducing training costs.

paragraphs: Inverse optimization uses observed decisions to estimate unknown parameters in an optimization model. Those estimates can then guide new decisions. This paper argues that committing to a single parameter estimate can be inadequate for that second step: the resulting recommendations may have poor quality or conflict with the decision maker's intuition, reducing their likelihood of adoption.

Conformal inverse optimization instead learns a set representing uncertainty about the unknown parameters. It uses that set in a robust optimization model to prescribe decisions. The change connects uncertainty in what was inferred from past choices to the process that generates future recommendations, making that uncertainty part of the decision problem.

Under mild assumptions, the authors prove guarantees on solution quality using two perspectives: the true parameters and the decision maker's perception of them. Experiments also show strong performance compared with classic inverse optimization. The contribution therefore concerns both the formal quality of recommendations and their alignment with how a decision maker understands the underlying problem.
neurips-2024-conformal-inverse-optimizat.tldr: Conformal inverse optimization learns parameter uncertainty and uses robust optimization to make decisions with conditional quality guarantees.

paragraphs: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy supports reconstruction of protein structures at near-atomic resolution. Its processing pipeline depends on tasks such as finding particles and estimating their poses, but training these components is constrained by a shortage of high-quality annotated datasets. CryoGEM addresses this bottleneck by generating synthetic microscopy data.

The method combines a physical simulation of imaging with a learned process for adding realistic noise. It first simulates images from a virtual specimen. It then uses unpaired noise translation, trained through contrastive learning and a mask-guided sampling scheme, to make the simulated data resemble noisy experimental images. The combination aims to preserve physical correctness while improving visual authenticity.

Extensive experiments show that CryoGEM can produce authentic cryo-EM images. The generated datasets can train particle-picking and pose-estimation models, ultimately improving reconstruction resolution. The significance is a connection between realistic synthetic training data and the quality of the reconstructed scientific structure, through the intermediate models that process the images.
neurips-2024-cryogem-physics-informed-ge.tldr: CryoGEM combines physical imaging simulation with learned realistic noise to generate training data that improves cryo-EM reconstruction.

paragraphs: This paper studies private optimization when each individual gradient is sparse, motivated by large embedding models. The distinction matters because the assumed sparsity belongs to individual gradients, rather than being a general claim that every quantity in training is sparse. The goal is to exploit that structure when establishing differential privacy guarantees and optimization accuracy.

The authors first develop nearly optimal bounds for estimating a mean from sparse data, with particular improvements in high dimensions. They also derive corresponding lower bounds using a new block-diagonal construction. Together, the achievable bounds and lower bounds characterize how close the proposed methods come to the best possible performance.

These results support nearly optimal algorithms for stochastic convex optimization under both pure and approximate differential privacy. The pure-private result gives the first nearly dimension-independent rates for this problem. For nonconvex empirical risk, new analyses of mean-estimation bias and randomly stopped biased stochastic gradient descent yield nearly dimension-independent rates for finding near-stationary points under approximate privacy.
neurips-2024-differentially-private-opti.tldr: Exploiting sparsity in individual gradients yields nearly optimal private optimization guarantees with reduced dependence on dimension.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models a distribution of possible returns, making the choice of how to compare distributions central to learning. The paper focuses on this comparison rule and its relationship to the representation of returns. It introduces SinkhornDRL, which uses Sinkhorn divergence, a regularized Wasserstein loss, to compare current return predictions with their Bellman targets.

The authors prove contraction properties for the proposed approach. These properties align with Sinkhorn divergence's position between Wasserstein distance and maximum mean discrepancy. The analysis also examines relationships with existing distributional methods, helping explain algorithm behavior through the distribution comparisons those methods use.

Experiments on the Atari suite show that SinkhornDRL consistently matches or exceeds existing algorithms in the reported evaluation. Its performance is especially strong when rewards have multiple dimensions. The result connects a theoretically analyzed comparison between return distributions to practical learning performance, while the multi-dimensional reward findings highlight a setting where the chosen divergence appears particularly useful.
neurips-2024-distributional-reinforcemen.tldr: SinkhornDRL uses a regularized Wasserstein loss to learn return distributions, with contraction guarantees and strong Atari results.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations offer a way to fuse multispectral and hyperspectral imagery, but they can lose high-frequency information and struggle to capture global context. FeINFN addresses these weaknesses by incorporating frequency information into the fusion process. Its design is motivated by a reported similarity in Fourier amplitudes between a high-resolution hyperspectral latent code and low-resolution hyperspectral imagery, alongside differences in their phases.

The network introduces a spatial and frequency implicit fusion function to capture high-frequency information and broaden the receptive field. It also uses a decoder with a complex Gabor wavelet activation to improve interactions among representation features. These components bring spatial and frequency processing together within the model.

The authors theoretically establish a time-frequency tightness property of the activation that favors learning suitable decoder bandwidths. On two benchmark fusion datasets, the method achieves state-of-the-art visual and quantitative results. Ablation studies support the contributions of the proposed components, connecting the architectural changes to the reported improvements.
neurips-2024-fourier-enhanced-implicit-n.tldr: FeINFN combines spatial and Fourier processing with a Gabor-activated decoder to improve multispectral and hyperspectral image fusion.

paragraphs: Generating images with diffusion models can require expensive numerical integration along a generative trajectory. Rectified flows try to simplify these paths so that fewer model evaluations are needed. This paper investigates how to train them effectively when generation uses only one or two evaluations, where existing rectified flows still faced a performance challenge.

The central finding is that, under realistic settings, one Reflow iteration is sufficient to learn nearly straight trajectories. The authors therefore improve training within that single round using a U-shaped timestep distribution and an LPIPS-Huber premetric. This focuses the approach on making one round effective rather than repeatedly applying Reflow.

On CIFAR-10, the changes improve FID by up to 75% relative to the previous 2-rectified flow in the single-evaluation setting. On ImageNet at 64 × 64 resolution, the method outperforms consistency and progressive distillation in one-step and two-step generation, while rivaling improved consistency training in FID. These results demonstrate competitive generation with very few evaluations.
neurips-2024-improving-the-training-of-r.tldr: Improved single-round rectified-flow training produces competitive images with just one or two model evaluations.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can answer questions about familiar scenes partly by relying on language patterns about what usually appears together. That makes strong benchmark scores an imperfect signal of detailed visual understanding. JourneyBench uses generated images of unusual imaginary situations to make those familiar expectations less useful.

The human-annotated benchmark covers five tasks: complementary multimodal chain of thought, questions involving multiple images, imaginary-image captioning, visual questions with hallucination triggers, and fine-grained retrieval with distractors tailored to each sample. Across these tasks, models must attend to specific visual evidence because an overall impression of the scene or a likely verbal answer is insufficient.

The authors evaluate state-of-the-art models and analyze performance across fine-grained dimensions. Results show that even the strongest tested models struggle across all five tasks. These findings challenge the interpretation of success on conventional benchmarks as evidence of equally strong visual reasoning. JourneyBench supplies a focused way to probe that gap using deliberately unusual scenarios.
neurips-2024-journeybench-a-challenging-.tldr: JourneyBench uses unusual generated scenes to expose weaknesses in vision-language reasoning that familiar-image benchmarks can obscure.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks hidden high-level variables and their causal relationships from observed data. Many identifiability results assume access to interventions on individual hidden variables. That is a demanding assumption when those variables are themselves unknown. This paper instead studies observations gathered from general environments.

The analysis focuses on the case where both the causal model and the mapping from latent variables to observations are linear. Even in that setting, the authors identify a largely unavoidable obstacle called surrounded-node ambiguity. This establishes a boundary on what can be uniquely recovered from the available environments, rather than promising complete identification.

Within the same linear setting, the authors show that recovery up to this ambiguity is possible under mild conditions. Their algorithm, LiNGCReL, provably achieves that guarantee. Extensive synthetic-data experiments also demonstrate its effectiveness with finite samples. The contribution combines a statement of intrinsic ambiguity with a constructive method that reaches the corresponding level of identifiability.
neurips-2024-learning-linear-causal-repr.tldr: LiNGCReL provably recovers linear causal representations up to an intrinsic ambiguity under mild conditions across general environments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes that the agent's state representation contains the information needed to predict dynamics and values. With partial observations, that assumption can fail. This paper introduces the lambda discrepancy to detect such failures and help learn useful memory without access to the hidden underlying state space.

The metric compares two temporal-difference value estimates computed with different lambda values. The motivation is that TD with lambda zero implicitly assumes a Markov representation, while TD with lambda one does not. The authors prove that the discrepancy is zero for all Markov decision processes and almost always nonzero for a broad class of partially observable environments.

The learning method uses two recurrent value networks and minimizes their disagreement as an auxiliary objective. Experiments show that reducing the discrepancy can help learn memory that mitigates partial observability. In the challenging domains evaluated, the resulting agent frequently performs significantly better than a recurrent baseline with one value network and never performs worse.
neurips-2024-mitigating-partial-observab.tldr: Disagreement between two temporal-difference value estimates can detect partial observability and guide an agent toward more useful memory.

paragraphs: Synthetic images can expand object-detection training datasets, but controlling their contents becomes difficult when scenes contain many object categories, dense arrangements, or occlusions. ODGEN addresses this challenge by generating images conditioned on bounding boxes, with a focus on matching the requirements of a particular detection domain.

Starting from a domain-specific dataset, the method fine-tunes a pretrained diffusion model on both cropped foreground objects and whole images. It then controls generation using synthesized visual prompts with spatial constraints and separate textual descriptions for individual objects. This combines adaptation to the target data with explicit guidance about object placement and content.

The authors evaluate a synthesis pipeline on seven domain-specific benchmarks. Adding generated data produces improvements of up to 25.3% in mAP@.50:.95 with detectors such as YOLOv5 and YOLOv7, outperforming earlier controllable generation methods. A separate COCO-2014 protocol reports an advantage of up to 5.6% on the same metric against existing methods, extending the evaluation to general domains.
neurips-2024-odgen-domain-specific-objec.tldr: ODGEN adapts and controls diffusion models to generate bounding-box-conditioned training images that improve object detection in evaluated domains.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model address a new task through its prompt without additional fine-tuning. This paper studies how that ability connects to semantic representations in which words encode multiple concepts with linear regularities. The goal is to mathematically explain how combining concepts can support performance on certain unseen tasks.

The analysis assumes a concept-based prompt model with low noise and sparse coding, inspired by empirical findings about latent semantic geometry. Within this setting, it incorporates softmax self-attention, ReLU-activated multilayer perceptrons, and cross-entropy training. These features let the theory address more of the transformer's actual nonlinear structure than the simplified settings discussed in the abstract.

The authors establish exponential convergence of zero-one loss through the nonconvex training dynamics and analyze out-of-distribution in-context learning. Simulations support the theoretical findings. The result explains a mechanism for generalization to certain tasks combining multiple concepts, with its guarantees tied to the stated prompt model rather than an unrestricted claim about all language-model reasoning.
neurips-2024-provably-transformers-harne.tldr: Under a low-noise sparse concept model, the paper proves how transformers can use multi-concept semantics for efficient in-context learning.

paragraphs: ScaleKD investigates whether strong pretrained vision transformers can teach models with different architectures, and whether stronger teachers deliver greater benefits. The authors identify three alignment problems: differences in how features are computed, differences in model scale, and differences in knowledge density. Addressing these mismatches is central to transferring useful information.

The method combines a cross-attention projector, dual-view feature mimicking, and teacher parameter perception. It trains student backbones spanning convolutional networks, multilayer perceptrons, and vision transformers. With a Swin-L teacher on ImageNet-1K, the reported absolute accuracy gains over independently trained students range from 2.02 to 5.52 percentage points across the listed architectures.

Experiments show larger student gains as teacher models or their pretraining datasets grow. The learned backbones also transfer well to MS-COCO and ADE20K. When a strong pretrained vision transformer is available, the authors propose ScaleKD as a more efficient alternative to extensive student pretraining, reporting reductions of up to 195 times in the number of training samples viewed.
neurips-2024-scalekd-strong-vision-trans.tldr: ScaleKD transfers knowledge from strong vision transformers to varied student architectures, with larger teachers producing larger empirical gains.

paragraphs: Practical score-based generative models face several errors at once: limited samples, imperfect learned scores, early stopping, and choices about training objectives and reference distributions. This paper develops a mathematical framework for tracking how such errors affect the generated distribution. Robustness here means bounding their distributional consequences.

The central Wasserstein uncertainty propagation theorem connects squared score-learning error to a Wasserstein-1 bound around the true data distribution under Fokker-Planck evolution. The resulting bounds use computable quantities and expose trade-offs between error sources. The proof draws on partial differential equation regularity and identifies the smoothing effect of stochastic diffusion as the mechanism supporting robustness.

The framework also extends to other distribution comparisons, including total variation and maximum mean discrepancy. Sample-complexity and generalization bounds follow from the theorem. The approach requires minimal assumptions, does not rely on the manifold hypothesis, and avoids requiring absolute continuity of the target distribution. This broadens the distributions covered by the analysis while providing a unified account of implementation errors.
neurips-2024-score-based-generative-mode.tldr: A new uncertainty-propagation theorem bounds how practical errors affect score-based generators and identifies stochastic diffusion as the robustness mechanism.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly participate in information retrieval, but they often serve as individual components inside systems built separately from them. The paper argues that this separation limits knowledge sharing and close coordination. Self-Retrieval reorganizes the process so that one language model performs the essential retrieval functions.

The model first internalizes the retrieval corpus through self-supervised learning. It then treats retrieval as sequential passage generation and assesses relevance to rerank the results. These stages place corpus learning, passage production, and relevance assessment within a shared model, creating an end-to-end architecture around the language model's capabilities.

The reported experiments show a significant improvement over existing retrieval approaches. They also show substantial gains in downstream language-model applications such as retrieval-augmented generation. This connects the architectural change to both retrieval performance and the usefulness of retrieved material in a broader application. The paper's contribution is therefore an integrated retrieval design with empirical benefits at both stages of use.
neurips-2024-self-retrieval-end-to-end-i.tldr: Self-Retrieval integrates corpus learning, passage retrieval, and reranking into one language model, improving retrieval and downstream applications in experiments.

paragraphs: SelfCodeAlign builds instruction-tuning data for code models without extensive human annotation or distillation from another model. It uses the same base model throughout generation, creating a transparent and permissive route to improving instruction following. The starting material is a collection of high-quality code snippets.

The pipeline extracts coding concepts from those snippets and turns them into new tasks. It samples several responses for each task, pairs them with tests, and checks them in a sandbox. Passing examples become training data. This makes executable validation part of deciding which generated responses the model should learn from.

Using CodeQwen1.5-7B, the authors create 74,000 instruction-response pairs and reach 67.1 pass@1 on HumanEval+, surpassing CodeLlama-70B-Instruct. The tuned model also consistently beats the OctoPack-trained version across the evaluated benchmarks. Additional experiments cover models from 3B to 33B parameters and support the value of using a model's own data distribution. The findings show that strong code instruction tuning can result from validated self-generated data.
neurips-2024-selfcodealign-self-alignmen.tldr: SelfCodeAlign improves code models by generating their own programming tasks and solutions, testing them, and training on passing examples.

paragraphs: Open-set 3D object retrieval must handle categories absent from training. This paper introduces a semi-open setting that distinguishes broad categories from fine-grained ones: training and test data share some coarse labels, while their fine labels are completely disjoint. That hierarchy captures overlap that a single layer of labels cannot adequately express.

The proposed HERT framework uses a Hierarchical Retrace Embedding module to exploit category information at multiple levels and address imbalance involving unseen categories. Its Structured Equilibrium Tuning module tackles overlapping features and category confusion. It constructs a superposed hypergraph from local coherent relationships and globally entangled relationships among objects.

The authors also create four datasets with multi-level labels for evaluating semi-open 3D retrieval. Results show that the framework can learn hierarchical object embeddings and generalize them to the proposed setting. The contribution joins a more differentiated evaluation problem with a representation method designed around it, making partial familiarity at the coarse level an explicit part of retrieval.
neurips-2024-semi-open-3d-object-retriev.tldr: HERT learns hierarchical 3D object representations for retrieval where broad categories partly overlap but fine-grained test categories are unseen.

paragraphs: Decentralized bilevel optimization involves agents solving nested optimization problems while communicating with their neighbors. Their data can differ, so the algorithm must correct for heterogeneity across agents. Existing approaches commonly use gradient tracking and apply the same decentralized strategy to both the upper and lower optimization levels.

SPARKLE provides a unified single-loop primal-dual framework that allows different heterogeneity-correction methods, including EXTRA and Exact Diffusion. It also permits the two optimization levels to use different strategies. This flexibility makes the choice of correction mechanism at each level an explicit algorithmic design decision.

The authors give a convergence analysis that applies across the framework's variants and establishes state-of-the-art rates relative to existing decentralized bilevel algorithms. Their results favor EXTRA and Exact Diffusion for this setting and show benefits from mixing strategies instead of using gradient tracking throughout. The significance is both a common theoretical treatment of several methods and evidence that nested optimization can benefit from different mechanisms at its two levels.
neurips-2024-sparkle-a-unified-single-lo.tldr: SPARKLE unifies decentralized bilevel algorithms and supports different heterogeneity corrections at each optimization level with strong convergence rates.

paragraphs: Exemplar-free class incremental learning trains a model on successive tasks without retaining access to earlier data. Some strong methods represent each class as a Gaussian distribution in the learned feature space. They use these distributions either for classification or for generating pseudo features to train a classifier.

The paper identifies two problems when the feature extractor changes during later tasks. Stored class covariance matrices also need to change, because they describe distributions in a space that is being updated. In addition, dimensionality collapse during training introduces a bias toward recent tasks. These issues affect both the class representations and the balance of predictions over time.

AdaGauss addresses them by adapting covariance matrices between tasks and adding an anti-collapse loss to mitigate recency bias. It achieves state-of-the-art results on the evaluated benchmarks with both training from scratch and pretrained backbones. The findings show the value of maintaining covariance information alongside the evolving representation and explicitly countering the collapse associated with recent-task preference.
neurips-2024-task-recency-bias-strikes-b.tldr: AdaGauss updates class covariances and counters feature collapse to improve incremental learning without access to past data.

paragraphs: Offline model-based reinforcement learning supplements a fixed dataset with synthetic trajectories from a learned dynamics model. It is natural to attribute failures to inaccuracies in that model. This paper challenges that explanation: in the authors' investigation, replacing learned dynamics with error-free dynamics causes existing methods to fail completely.

The explanation concerns rollout length. Theoretical treatments assume full-horizon trajectories, while practical algorithms truncate rollouts to avoid accumulating model error. Truncation creates edge-of-reach states where value learning relies on estimates without adequate support. Those estimates can become severely inflated, leading to performance collapse even when the dynamics themselves are correct.

The authors revise the theoretical account and argue that earlier methods primarily manage this edge-of-reach problem, despite being described as remedies for model inaccuracy. They introduce Reach-Aware Value Learning to address it directly. The method avoids the reported failure as dynamics improve, showing why more accurate world models also require value-learning procedures that handle the boundaries of synthetic experience.
neurips-2024-the-edge-of-reach-problem-i.tldr: Truncated model rollouts can cause unsupported value estimates and collapse even with perfect dynamics; RAVL directly addresses this boundary problem.

paragraphs: Large graphs can become expensive to store, process, and analyze. Graph coarsening reduces their size while trying to preserve important structural properties, including spectral information. The paper identifies a coverage problem in existing methods: most are suited to homophilic datasets, limiting their usefulness across different patterns of relationships.

Universal Graph Coarsening is designed for both homophilic and heterophilic datasets. It combines node attributes with adjacency information and incorporates the dataset's heterophily factor. This brings information about the nodes and the pattern of their connections into the same coarsening framework, allowing the approach to address both kinds of dataset.

On benchmark datasets, UGC preserves spectral similarity and has lower eigen-error than existing methods. It is also reported to be four to fifteen times faster and to deliver better downstream performance even at 70% coarsening ratios. These findings assess compression through several connected outcomes: computational cost, retained graph structure, and the usefulness of the smaller graph for subsequent tasks.
neurips-2024-ugc-universal-graph-coarsen.tldr: UGC combines node attributes and connectivity to coarsen homophilic and heterophilic graphs while preserving useful structure and improving processing speed.

paragraphs: Discrete disease progression models infer the order in which patient features become measurably abnormal. This ordering describes a group-level trajectory and can support disease staging. Traditional maximum-likelihood inference becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of features grows, because the number of possible event orderings expands combinatorially.

The paper uses ideas from optimal transport to represent event ordering through a latent permutation matrix in the Birkhoff polytope. It performs inference by optimizing a variational lower bound. The authors report inference 1,000 times faster than the current state of the art, enabling models with several orders of magnitude more features.

Simulations show improvements in speed, accuracy, and robustness to noise. Experiments on separate Alzheimer's disease and age-related macular degeneration imaging datasets demonstrate pixel-level progression events in the brain and eye. This makes much finer-grained event modeling feasible. The method's low computational requirements and interpretability support broad potential clinical utility, with the reported real-data demonstrations covering these two disease settings.
neurips-2024-unscrambling-disease-progre.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation dramatically accelerates disease-event ordering, enabling pixel-level progression models in brain and eye imaging.
